claims.text: A data-driven approach incorporating atomic-scale lattice-disorder descriptors will identify single-phase high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than conventional empirical methods.
Atomic-mass variation and bonding-strength variation are useful descriptors of lattice disorder for predicting phonon thermal conductivity.
Intrinsic randomness in atomic sizes and bonding environments enhances phonon scattering in disordered HEAs.
The applicable materials are chemically homogeneous, single-phase HEAs, including disordered BCC or FCC alloys, with significant atomic-mass and bonding variability.
The model will screen and select HEA compositions using computed lattice-disorder and bonding descriptors.
Secondary phases and oxide or carbide contamination can alter thermal transport.
Atomic-scale lattice disorder and bond-strength variation enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by lattice and bond disorder reduces phonon thermal conductivity.
A random distribution of elements having different masses and bonding characteristics disrupts phonon propagation through scattering.
Quantifying local lattice fluctuations permits more precise estimation of phonon scattering and phonon thermal conductivity than approaches based on averaged parameters.
Within the stated applicability regime, the model will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20% or more relative to traditional empirical methods.
Conventional baseline approaches use averaged lattice parameters and empirical correlations without representing the full spectrum of atomic-scale disorder in HEAs.
The predictive approach will be less reliable for multiphase alloys or alloys with substantial processing-induced oxide or carbide contamination.
Multiphase microstructures or contamination disrupt the homogeneous-lattice-disorder assumption underlying the model.
The proposed 20% accuracy improvement has not been firmly established.
The model's performance outside the single-phase regime is uncertain.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant and approximately 20% improvement in prediction accuracy over the conventional baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis defines success as improved prediction accuracy, but parts of the benchmark instead compare whether selected alloys have lower conductivity. Lower measured conductivity does not by itself demonstrate lower prediction error, and the falsification rule conflates a reduction in conductivity with a percentage improvement in predictive accuracy.
